options.content:
# W&B Application

Answers **"is the whole W&B app slow or erroring for this customer?"** Start here when a customer reports the UI is slow, requests fail, or the SDK can't reach the server.

The top sections cover **overall API health** — request rate and errors overall and by request type (`graphql`, `files`, filestream, …), and latency. The **GraphQL errors** section attributes failures to the specific service/operation responsible. The **Operations & background** section shows read-path, artifact, and export span latencies from traces. The **Run Keys** section shows how many distinct metric keys active runs log, with recommended limits by instance size. The **FileStream** section shows whether live run logging (history, events, console logs) is failing or slow.

Use the **W&B Namespace** dropdown to pick the customer's install. Use **Open Traces in Explore** (top-right) to drill from any symptom to a real trace.

panels.title: About: Request rate by status code

options.content:
**What it shows** — every HTTP request the W&B API serves, per second, split by response code. This is the single best "is the app up?" view.

**What bad looks like** — a wall of `5xx` appearing, or `2xx` dropping to near-zero (traffic no longer reaching the API: ingress / service / DNS / pod crash).

**Do next** — 5xx climbing → check pod logs. To attribute GraphQL errors to a feature, see the **GraphQL errors** section below.

**What it shows** — client errors (`4xx`) vs server errors (`5xx`) as two clean lines, so you can tell whose fault it is.

**What bad looks like** — any sustained `5xx` is a server problem. A `4xx` spike is usually the customer's SDK/auth (version mismatch, bad token, malformed query) and is often *not* an outage.

**Do next** — 5xx → check API pod logs. 4xx → confirm SDK version against **Service Image Versions** on [W&B Field Investigation](/d/wandb-field-investigation).

**Note** — GraphQL errors return HTTP `200` (the error is in the response body), so they don't appear here; use the **GraphQL errors** section below for those. This panel catches HTTP transport/server failures; a flat `0` means healthy.

**What it shows** — the share of requests failing with a server error, as a percentage. Normalizes for traffic so a busy install and a quiet one read the same.

**What bad looks like** — above ~1% sustained is a real incident; a brief blip during a deploy is usually fine.

**Do next** — if the ratio is high, capture a snapshot of this panel and use the **GraphQL errors** section below to see which feature is responsible, then drill to a trace.

**Note** — this is HTTP `5xx` only; GraphQL errors are HTTP `200`, so a `0` ratio doesn't mean error-free — check the **GraphQL errors** section below.

panels.title: HTTP request rate by request type (top 10)
panels.description: Requests per second the W&B api deployment handles, by request type (route), excluding Kubernetes health probes. Statsd samples arrive as 15s deltas, so the rate uses rate_over_sum.

panels.title: About: Request rate by request type

options.content:
**What it shows** — the same requests as **Request rate by status code** above, split by what was asked for: `graphql` (the UI and most SDK calls), `files` (uploads and downloads), filestream (live run logging), and so on. Kubernetes health probes (`healthz`, `ready`) are left out so they don't hide real traffic.

**What bad looks like** — one request type jumping far above its usual rate (a script or many runs hammering one endpoint), or a type that's normally busy dropping to zero while users are active (that path is broken or not reaching the server).

**Do next** — a high rate alone is load, not a fault. Check the error panel below for the same request type, and the **Latency** section for whether the server is keeping up. GraphQL traffic is broken down by operation in **GraphQL operations (all requests)** further down.

panels.title: HTTP 4xx / 5xx rate by request type
panels.description: Failed requests per second by request type and HTTP status code, 4xx and 5xx only. Statsd samples arrive as 15s deltas, so the rate uses rate_over_sum.

options.content:
**What it shows** — which request types are failing, and with which status code. Use it to turn "we're seeing errors" into "`files` is returning `503`".

**What bad looks like** — any sustained `5xx` line is a server-side problem on that path. A `4xx` line is usually the client: an expired API key (`401`), missing permissions (`403`), an old SDK sending a bad request (`400`). A few `graphql 400`s are normal background noise.

**Do next** — `5xx` on one request type → check the `api` pod logs for that route and the backing service it uses (object storage for `files`, MySQL for `graphql`). A burst of `401` / `403` → ask the user to check their API key and team membership.

**Note** — GraphQL errors return HTTP `200`, so they don't appear here; see the **GraphQL errors** section below.

**What it shows** — how long requests take, across all gorilla requests. p50 is the typical user; p95/p99 are the slowest 5% / 1%.

**What bad looks like** — p95 above ~3s sustained for more than a few minutes means users feel it. Brief spikes under load are tolerable.

**Do next** — if p95/p99 are high, use **p95 by operation** and **Top operations by slow request count** below to find the culprit, then Open Traces in Explore (top-right) and filter `duration>3s`.

**What it shows** — the 10 operations (trace span names) with the highest p95 latency, over time. Tells you *which operation* is slow, not just that something is. Sourced from spanmetrics (`traces_spanmetrics_*`, milliseconds) since gorilla's HTTP metrics don't carry a route label.

**What bad looks like** — one operation sitting well above the rest, especially graphql spans climbing after a deploy.

**Do next** — a slow graphql span → see the **GraphQL errors** section below; a slow read/export span → see **Operations & background** below. Then drill to a trace for that operation.

panels.title: Top operations by slow request count (>2.5s)
About: Top operations by slow request count

options.content:
**What it shows** — the operations that produced the most requests slower than 2.5 seconds over the selected range (counted from the latency histogram). This is the volume view of slowness: which operations hurt the most users.

**What bad looks like** — an operation with a large, growing count of >2.5s requests, especially the workspace, run-table, or artifact operations.

**Do next** — note the top operation, Open Traces in Explore (top-right), filter `service.name=gorilla` and `duration>2.5s` on that operation to read a real slow trace.

panels.title: GraphQL operation rate by span (top, sampled)
panels.description: From spanmetrics (traces), which are sampled — trust the shape, not the absolute count. Spanmetrics have NO namespace label, so this is not filtered by $namespace; it reflects the whole trace stream.

options.content:
**What it shows** — the busiest GraphQL operations by request rate, from sampled traces. Good for seeing *what the customer's app is doing* and whether a particular operation surged.

**What bad looks like** — one operation dominating far above normal (a client hot-loop or retry storm), or the whole stream going flat (traffic stopped).

**Do next** — for *errors* by GraphQL service/operation, see the **GraphQL errors** section below. Note: spanmetrics have no namespace label, so this is not scoped to the selected install.

panels.title: GraphQL p95 latency by span (sampled)
panels.description: From spanmetrics (traces), which are sampled. Spanmetrics have NO namespace label, so this is not filtered by $namespace.

options.content:
**What it shows** — the slowest GraphQL operations at p95, in milliseconds, from sampled traces.

**What bad looks like** — an operation's p95 climbing into the seconds, especially if it lines up with the customer's complaint.

**Do next** — Open Traces in Explore (top-right), filter to that operation, and read the resolver chain. For error attribution by service, see the **GraphQL errors** section below.

**What it shows** — top-line GraphQL error health, from sampled traces (trust the trend, not the exact count).

**What bad looks like** — *distinct erroring services* jumping from ~1 to many (a broad outage vs. one bad dependency), or the error count climbing off a flat baseline.

**Do next** — one service dominating → look at **Attribution by service** below and open its trace via **Open Traces in Explore** (top-right).

**What it shows** — which GraphQL **service** (schema source file) and which **operation** are producing errors, from sampled traces. The `graphql.service` label rides on gorilla's spans (core PR #43519).

**What bad looks like** — one service far above the rest = a single dependency/resolver in trouble; errors spread evenly across many services = something shared (DB, auth, rate-limiter).

**Do next** — note the top service/operation, then **Open Traces in Explore** (top-right), filter to gorilla + `error=true` and that operation name, and read the resolver chain / error message on the actual trace. If this panel is empty, the spanmetrics `graphql.service` dimension may not be flowing yet — confirm traces reach the gateway and the collector was restarted after the dimension was added.

panels.title: GraphQL errors per minute, by service (sampled)

options.content:
**What it shows** — the same service attribution over time, stacked so you can see *when* a service started erroring and whether it correlates with a deploy.

**What bad looks like** — a service's band appearing or ballooning at a specific minute.

**Do next** — line up the onset time with the **Service Image Versions** panel on [W&B Field Investigation](/d/wandb-field-investigation) (a rollout?) and with the customer's report. Then drill to a trace from that window.

**Get to the cause in three hops:** (1) identify the top service/operation above → (2) **Open Traces in Explore** (top-right), filter `service.name` to gorilla, `error=true`, and the operation → (3) read the resolver chain and error message on the actual trace. If gorilla's OTEL log export is enabled, follow **Trace → Logs** from there to the correlated log lines.

panels.title: History-reader span latency p95 (traces, sampled)
panels.description: Trace-derived (traces_spanmetrics_*, confirmed present) so it is SAMPLED — trust the shape, not exact values. The span_name regex is a best guess; if this panel is empty, run label_values(traces_spanmetrics_duration_milliseconds_bucket, span_name) and adjust the regex to the history-reader / clickhouse span names on your stack.

options.content:
**What it shows** — p95 duration of the read-path spans (history reader / ClickHouse query) from sampled traces, split by span. Answers "why won't the customer's charts load?"

**What bad looks like** — one span's p95 climbing into seconds, or a new span appearing at a specific minute.

**Do next** — note the slow span and the minute it started, then **Open Traces in Explore** (top-right) and read the actual span chain. If the panel is empty, the span-name regex needs adjusting (see the panel description).

panels.title: Artifact operation latency p95 (traces, sampled)
panels.description: Trace-derived (traces_spanmetrics_*, confirmed present) so it is SAMPLED — trust the shape, not exact values. The span_name regex matches any span containing 'artifact'; if this panel is empty, run label_values(traces_spanmetrics_duration_milliseconds_bucket, span_name) and adjust the regex to the artifact span names on your stack.

options.content:
**What it shows** — p95 latency of artifact-related spans from sampled traces, split by span. Answers "why is the customer's artifact upload/download slow?"

**What bad looks like** — one artifact span's p95 climbing into seconds.

**Do next** — to see an individual slow artifact request end to end, use the **Open Traces in Explore** link (top-right), set the service to gorilla and filter for `duration > 3s` and an artifact operation, then read the span chain. If this panel is empty, adjust the span-name regex (see the panel description).

panels.title: Top parquet/glue spans by call count (sampled)

options.content:
**What it shows** — trace-derived (spanmetrics) call counts for spans whose name mentions parquet or glue. This is the background export/compaction work as seen from tracing.

**Note** — spanmetrics are **not** namespace-scoped and are **sampled**: trust the *shape* (which span dominates), not exact counts.

**Do next** — to see an actual slow/failed export, use **Open Traces in Explore** (top-right) and filter by the span name shown here. If this panel is empty, the span name pattern may differ on your stack — check `label_values(traces_spanmetrics_calls_total, span_name)`.

panels.title: Keys per run — P50 / P90 / P99
panels.description: Distribution of each run's total distinct keys, recorded by flat-run-fields-updater whenever a run's keys_info changes (impl=v2). Metrics arrive as 15s deltas, so queries use sum_over_time / rate_over_sum rather than rate().

options.content:
### What is this?

How many distinct metric keys active runs have. Each sample is a run's **total** keys when its keys_info updates, so runs that log often count more.

### Why it matters

A large number of unique metrics in one run can slow:
- **SDK:** live run updates, end-of-run sync
- **Project workspace:** runs table, charts
- **Run workspace:** run overview, charts
- **Reports:** run sets

It can also put disproportionate load on MySQL and affect performance across the app.

### What to do

This measures user activity, not a fault. If **p99** is above the limit for this instance's size (see the table below):
1. Work with the user to understand the use case and whether that many keys per step are needed.
2. If they are, size the infrastructure for that run cardinality.

Source: `mysql_metadata.keys_info.keys_items{impl="v2"}`, W&B server statsd emitted by the `flat-run-fields-updater` deployment.

panels.title: Keys per run — average and update rate
Run Keys: recommended limits by instance size

options.content:
Compare **p99 keys per run** with the row for this instance's size. If it's consistently above the limit, review the use case with the user, or move up a size. Each step up mainly adds MySQL capacity; Medium → Large and X-Large → XX-Large also increase compute and cache.

| Size | Max keys per run | AWS DB node | GCP DB node | Azure DB node | On-prem, operator-managed MySQL (per replica, 3 replicas) | Bare metal, external MySQL host |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Small | 1k | r6g.large | db-n1-highmem-2 | E2ds_v4 | 2 vCPU / 8 GiB, 100 GiB disk | 2 vCPU / 16 GB |
| Medium | 25k | r6g.xlarge | db-n1-highmem-4 | E4ds_v4 | 4 vCPU / 16 GiB, 200 GiB disk | 4 vCPU / 32 GB |
| Large | 50k | r6g.2xlarge | db-n1-highmem-8 | E8ds_v4 | 8 vCPU / 30 GiB, 500 GiB disk | 8 vCPU / 64 GB |
| X-Large | 75k | r6g.4xlarge | db-n1-highmem-16 | E16ds_v4 | 15 vCPU / 60 GiB, 1 TiB disk | 16 vCPU / 128 GB |
| XX-Large | 100k | r6g.8xlarge | db-n1-highmem-32 | E32ds_v4 | 30 vCPU / 120 GiB, 2 TiB disk | 32 vCPU / 256 GB |

The on-prem column is the operator v2 `mysql` sizing profile. The bare-metal column matches the cloud DB node for the same size; use fast local NVMe storage.

panels.title: FileStream write errors / sec
panels.description: Failed writes of live run data to the FileStream store (MySQL) per second, by service. On-prem these come from the api deployment, shown as service "gorilla". Statsd samples arrive as 15s deltas, so the rate uses rate_over_sum. The errors counter only exists once an error has happened, hence the 'or vector(0)' total.

options.content:
**What it shows** — writes of live run data (history, events, console logs) to the FileStream store that failed. The `api` deployment does these writes. Answers "are users' runs delaying logged data?"

**What bad looks like** — anything sustained above zero. A failed write means the SDK retries, so users see charts stall.

**Do next** — confirm whether users' (AI engineers') runs are losing or delaying logged data, and check **Request latency (p50 / p95 / p99)** above, which should also rise if writes are delayed. Then check the `api` pod's logs in VictoriaLogs for the error, and the backing store (MySQL, ClickHouse or object storage).

panels.title: FileStream write error rate
panels.description: Failed FileStream store writes divided by all FileStream store writes.

options.content:
**What it shows** — the share of FileStream store writes that failed.

**What bad looks like** — a sustained non-zero rate. A low rate under heavy load is a different problem from a high rate with few writes: compare with the errors/sec panel above.

**Do next** — same as write errors. If the rate jumps at a specific minute, line it up with the MySQL and storage panels on the Telemetry Overview.

panels.title: FileStream P50 Latency
panels.description: Median time the api pod takes to write one batch of live run data to the FileStream store (MySQL on-prem).

panels.title: FileStream Ingest Latency
panels.description: P50 / P90 / P99 time from the api pod accepting a batch of live run data to that batch landing in the FileStream store (MySQL on-prem): the lag users see between logging and charts updating. Buckets use VictoriaMetrics' vmrange label; quantiles use sum_over_time because statsd samples are 15s deltas.

options.content:
**What it shows** — server-side FileStream ingest latency: how long the W&B `api` pod takes to write each batch of logged run data (history, events, console logs) to the FileStream store (MySQL on-prem).

**What bad looks like** — P99 climbing into seconds, or P50 rising with load. Under healthy load P50 typically stays below 50 ms.

**Do next** — P50 and P99 rising together: MySQL is slow. Check queries/s, row locks, buffer pool and connections vs max on the Telemetry Overview. P99 spiking alone: check that pod's CPU throttling and restarts/OOMs (Workload Resources) before blaming the database, then row-lock time.

panels.title: FileStream lines per write (p50 / p99)
panels.description: Lines carried by each FileStream store write, by item type (history, event, log).

options.content:
**What it shows** — how many lines of history, events or console logs each write carries.

**What bad looks like** — p99 jumping well above normal: a few runs are logging very large batches, which slows their writes and can hold up others.

**Do next** — if latency rose at the same time, find the heavy runs (see the Run Keys section above) and check their logging pattern with the user.

panels.title: Active-run updates from FileStream
panels.description: Run-metadata updates per second made by the flat-run-fields-updater deployment (shown as service "gorilla-flat-run-fields-updater") as live run data arrives, roughly how many active runs are sending updates, plus failures.

options.content:
**What it shows** — run-metadata updates driven by FileStream (summary, step, heartbeat). It tracks how many runs are actively logging.

**What bad looks like** — errors above zero, or the update rate dropping while users say runs are still training (updates aren't getting through).

**Do next** — check flat-run-fields-updater logs in VictoriaLogs and MySQL load. A high, steady update rate is normal for many concurrent runs, not a fault.

panels.title: GraphQL request rate by operation (top 10)
panels.description: GraphQL requests per second by operation, counted by the W&B api deployment. Unlike the sampled span panels above, this counts every request. Statsd samples arrive as 15s deltas, so the rate uses rate_over_sum.

options.content:
**What it shows** — every GraphQL request the W&B `api` deployment handles, per second, for the 10 busiest operations. The W&B UI and the SDK both talk to the server through GraphQL, so this is the clearest picture of what users are asking the server to do.

**What bad looks like** — one operation jumping far above its usual rate (a script or a browser tab polling in a loop), or the whole graph going flat while users say they're working (requests aren't reaching the server — check ingress and the `api` pods).

**Do next** — a high rate on its own is load, not a fault. Line it up with the latency panels below: if latency rises with the rate, the server or MySQL is running out of headroom. `UpsertBucket` spikes usually mean many runs starting at once (`wandb.init()`).

panels.title: GraphQL P50 latency by operation (top 10)
panels.description: Median GraphQL response time by operation, in seconds, for the 10 slowest operations. Statsd samples arrive as 15s deltas, so buckets are summed with sum_over_time before histogram_quantile.

panels.title: GraphQL P90 latency by operation (top 10)
panels.description: P90 GraphQL response time by operation, in seconds, for the 10 slowest operations. Statsd samples arrive as 15s deltas, so buckets are summed with sum_over_time before histogram_quantile.

options.content:
**What it shows** — how long the server takes to answer each GraphQL operation. P50 is a typical request; P90 is what the slowest 1 in 10 users wait for, and is the better signal for "the UI feels slow".

**What bad looks like** — P90 above a few seconds on operations behind pages people use: `RunSelectorRuns` / `HistoryKeys*` (runs table), `*DeltaQuery*` (live charts), `ProjectArtifacts` / `RunArtifactVersions` (artifacts). Large projects are naturally slower, so compare against this install's normal, not zero.

**Do next** — P50 and P90 rising together across many operations: the backend is saturated. Check **MetadataStore latency** and **MySQL connection pool** below, then MySQL on the Telemetry Overview. One operation slow while others are fine: open Traces in Explore, filter to that operation, and read where the time goes.

panels.title: MetadataStore operation rate by service (top 10)

targets.expr: topk(10, sum by (component, operation) (label_replace(label_replace(sum by (__name__, operation) (rate_over_sum({__name__=~"gorilla_.*MetadataStore_operation_duration_count", namespace="$namespace"}[$__rate_interval]) keep_metric_names), "component", "$1", "__name__", "gorilla_?(.*?)_?MetadataStore_.*"), "component", "api", "component", "")))

panels.description: MetadataStore (MySQL) operations per second, by W&B service and operation. The service comes from the metric name (gorilla_<service>_MetadataStore_...); 'api' is the api deployment. Statsd samples arrive as 15s deltas, so the rate uses rate_over_sum.

options.content:
**What it shows** — the database reads and writes each W&B service makes through its MetadataStore (runs, projects, users, artifacts metadata in MySQL), per second. It shows *which service* is putting load on MySQL.

**What bad looks like** — one service or operation suddenly dominating, or a steady rise that tracks MySQL CPU or queries/s on the Telemetry Overview.

**Do next** — find the service here, then check its pods under Workload Resources on the Telemetry Overview. A surge in write operations alongside many new runs is expected load; a surge with no change in user activity is worth raising with W&B support.

panels.title: MetadataStore P50 latency by operation (top 10)

targets.expr: topk(10, histogram_quantile(0.5, sum by (vmrange, component, operation) (label_replace(label_replace(sum by (__name__, vmrange, operation) (sum_over_time({__name__=~"gorilla_.*MetadataStore_operation_duration_bucket", namespace="$namespace"}[$__rate_interval]) keep_metric_names), "component", "$1", "__name__", "gorilla_?(.*?)_?MetadataStore_.*"), "component", "api", "component", ""))))

panels.description: Median MetadataStore operation time, in seconds, for the 10 slowest service/operation pairs. Statsd samples arrive as 15s deltas, so buckets are summed with sum_over_time before histogram_quantile.

panels.title: MetadataStore P90 latency by operation (top 10)

targets.expr: topk(10, histogram_quantile(0.9, sum by (vmrange, component, operation) (label_replace(label_replace(sum by (__name__, vmrange, operation) (sum_over_time({__name__=~"gorilla_.*MetadataStore_operation_duration_bucket", namespace="$namespace"}[$__rate_interval]) keep_metric_names), "component", "$1", "__name__", "gorilla_?(.*?)_?MetadataStore_.*"), "component", "api", "component", ""))))

panels.description: P90 MetadataStore operation time, in seconds, for the 10 slowest service/operation pairs. Statsd samples arrive as 15s deltas, so buckets are summed with sum_over_time before histogram_quantile.

options.content:
**What it shows** — how long W&B services wait on MySQL for each kind of operation. This is the database as the application sees it, including time waiting for a connection.

**What bad looks like** — P90 in the hundreds of milliseconds or more on operations that are normally fast.

**Do next** — many operations slow at once: MySQL is overloaded or the pool is exhausted. Check the connection pool panels below, then queries/s, buffer pool hit % and connections vs max_connections on the Telemetry Overview. One or two operations slow while others are fine (often writes such as `UpsertBucket`): suspect row-lock contention, so check **InnoDB Row Lock Time** on the Telemetry Overview.

panels.title: MySQL connections in use / idle by service
panels.description: Open MySQL connections per W&B service, split into in use and idle, summed across that service's pods. From the OpenTelemetry database/sql instrumentation (db_sql_connection_open).

panels.title: MySQL connection pool utilisation by service

targets.expr: 100 * sum by (service_name) (db_sql_connection_open{k8s_namespace_name="$namespace", service_name=~"gorilla.*", status="inuse"}) / sum by (service_name) (db_sql_connection_max_open{k8s_namespace_name="$namespace", service_name=~"gorilla.*"})

panels.description: Connections in use as a share of the pool limit (db_sql_connection_max_open), per W&B service, across all of that service's pods.

options.content:
**What it shows** — each W&B service keeps a pool of MySQL connections. *In use* are running a query now; *idle* are open and ready. Utilisation is in-use as a share of the pool limit (by default 100 per pod).

**What bad looks like** — utilisation near 100% with idle near zero: the pool is exhausted and new requests queue for a connection (see **wait pressure** below). This is usually the first thing to check when MySQL "looks slow".

**Do next** — high utilisation with slow MetadataStore latency: MySQL itself is slow to answer, so check MySQL on the Telemetry Overview before raising pool sizes. Also compare the total across services with MySQL `max_connections` on the Telemetry Overview — raising pools or replicas past that limit just moves the queue into MySQL.

panels.title: MySQL connection waits / sec by service
panels.description: How often a request had to wait for a free MySQL connection, per second, by W&B service (db_sql_connection_wait_total).

panels.title: MySQL connection avg wait time by service
panels.description: Average time a request waited for a MySQL connection, in ms, by W&B service. Shows 0 when nothing waited.

options.content:
**What it shows** — requests that found every connection in the pool busy and had to wait, and how long they waited.

**What bad looks like** — any sustained waits above zero. Waits mean users are queuing for the database before their query even starts, and it shows up as higher latency everywhere.

**Do next** — confirm with **pool utilisation** above. Then check whether MySQL is slow (Telemetry Overview: queries/s, row lock time, buffer pool) — slow queries hold connections longer and drain the pool. If MySQL is healthy and waits persist under normal load, contact W&B support about pool sizing for this install.

panels.title: MySQL connections closed by pool limits / sec
panels.description: Connections the pool closed per second because of its own settings (max lifetime, max idle count, max idle time), by W&B service.

panels.title: About: Connections closed by pool limits

options.content:
**What it shows** — connections the pool closed on purpose: too old (*max lifetime*), too many idle (*max idle*), or idle too long (*max idle time*).

**What bad looks like** — a high, steady *max lifetime* or *max idle* rate during busy periods: the pool keeps tearing down and reopening connections, which adds connection-setup load on MySQL.

**Do next** — a low background rate is normal. If it's high, compare with **Connections vs max_connections** and MySQL CPU on the Telemetry Overview, and share it with W&B support when reporting slowness.
